newsitem.title: USA: Kmart takes Manhattan; will Manhattan take Kmart?
newsitem.headline: Kmart takes Manhattan; will Manhattan take Kmart?

text.p: Kmart Corp. opened its first Manhattan store on Wednesday, bringing its heralded low prices to a city renowned more for Fifth Avenue fashion than discount retailing.
Model Kathy Ireland, who endorses a line of clothes for Kmart, and Chief Executive Officer Floyd Hall welcomed an army of eager shoppers who poured in once the red ribbon was cut to open the store.
Industry analysts said the store stood a good chance of becoming a hit with New Yorkers despite the unimpressive record of discounters who have tried to make it in Manhattan.

"I think there is a major need for this type of store in Manhattan. Kmart recently opened a store in Queens and that ranks very highly in terms of volume for the entire chain," said Joseph Ronning, retail analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman. "It's clearly an issue of population density."
He said that while rent and operating costs would be high, they would be balanced out by the high volume of sales.

Other analysts said the heavily trafficked location would help. The store is next door to Penn Station and the Long Island Railroad and in the midst of a shopping mecca anchored by Macy's 34th Street flagship store.

Kmart, known for unadvertised sales that lasted 15 minutes and became known as "blue-light specials," opened its first store in 1962 in Detroit. With 2,144 stores, 28 of them outside the United States, Kmart is the nation's third largest retailer.

Kmart follows in the footsteps of Bradlees Inc., which has a store in nearby Union Square, and E.J. Korvette, one of the first major discount chains whose New York experiment failed in the late 1960s.
All in all, the city has not been friendly to big stores and many chains have been reluctant to settle here because of high rents and what retailers call inventory shrinkage, or theft.
Its New York challenge aside, Kmart has struggled in recent years.
In August it reported a profit in its second quarter, ending a string of 13 consecutive quarterly losses.

Bradlees, in addition to its problems at the New York store, has had other troubles that drove it into Chapter 11 bankruptcy, where it is trying to reorganize. Analysts said it never adapted inventory to the needs of Manhattanites.

"They did not really tailor their assortment to the market. They were trying to sell stuff to apartment dwellers that would be more suitable to the suburbs, snow plows and things like that," one analyst said.
Another noted failure, Korvette made a different sort of error, according to Kurt Barnard, president of Barnard's Retail Marketing Report, a forecasting firm. It forgot that it was a discount store.
"They decided they wanted a store on Fifth Avenue. They jacked up prices and stopped operating like a discount store," he said.

Hall, who lives in the New York area and commutes to his job at Kmart headquarters in Troy, Mich., said Kmart would not be making those errors and that it had adapted its various departments to the needs of New Yorkers and is banning the sale of firearms, both real and toys, in the Manhattan store.
"We spoke to law enforcement agencies and they felt strongly about firearm sales, both real and toys," Hall told Reuters. "We have a strong community feeling."
He said business considerations also played a part in the decision and that in suburban stores where many shoppers include hunters, the situation was different.
Hall also said that such departments as sporting goods and lawnmowers have been reduced while the selection of rollerblades has been expanded in the Manhattan store.
Shoppers adopted an it's-about-time attitude as they made their first forays into the new store, which in addition to a ground floor has two subterranean shopping levels.
"Kmart in the city," said Alicia Gaines, a Wall Street trader who was among the first to shop in the new store, located next to the Madison Square Garden arena.
"It's like when they first brought hot dogs to street corners. You have got to have one," she said.
